questions.question: On a break-even chart, the region to the LEFT of the break-even point, between the total cost and total revenue lines, represents:
questions.explanation: To the left of the break-even point total cost is above total revenue, so the gap between them is a loss; to the right TR exceeds TC and the gap is profit. Option C describes the right-hand region, option B measures how far sales are above break-even, and option A is a per-unit figure, not an area on the chart.

questions.question: If a firm increases its selling price per unit while fixed cost and variable cost per unit stay the same, its break-even point in units will:
questions.explanation: A higher price raises contribution per unit (P - V), so fewer units are needed to cover the same fixed cost, and BEP = FC / (P - V) falls; on the chart the TR line becomes steeper and the break-even point moves left. Option D would follow a fall in price or a rise in costs, option A ignores the change in contribution, and option C mixes units with naira.

questions.question: If the variable cost per unit rises while selling price and fixed cost stay the same, the break-even point in units will:
questions.explanation: A higher variable cost reduces contribution per unit (P - V), so more units are needed to recover the same fixed cost and BEP = FC / (P - V) rises. Option A would follow a rise in price or a fall in variable cost, option D ignores that contribution has changed, and option C could only happen if fixed cost were zero.

questions.question: Margin, as a pricing measure, expresses profit as a percentage of:

options.a: total revenue of the whole firm

questions.explanation: Margin (%) = (Selling Price - Cost) / Selling Price x 100, so its base is the selling price. Option D is the base for mark-up, which is why mark-up is the larger figure for a profitable item, while options C and A are not used as the base for either measure.

questions.question: For the same principal and interest rate over a period longer than one year, annual compound interest compared with simple interest gives:

options.b: a larger amount only when the rate is above 10%

questions.explanation: From the second year onward compound interest earns interest on interest already added, so it always accumulates more than simple interest over more than one year at any positive rate. Option C is only true for exactly one year, option D has it backwards, and option B adds a condition that does not exist.

questions.question: Logarithms are best described as:

options.a: the inverse of indices, used to simplify exponential calculations
options.b: equations whose variables are raised only to the first power
options.c: statements of constraints using signs such as less than or equal to
options.d: two or more equations solved together for several unknowns

questions.explanation: A logarithm is the inverse of an index (power) and simplifies exponential calculations such as continuous growth. Option B describes linear equations, option C describes linear inequalities, and option D describes simultaneous equations.

questions.question: Company X has a margin of safety of 3,000 units while Company Y, in the same industry, has a margin of safety of 200 units. What does this tell management?

options.a: Company X's fixed costs must be lower than Company Y's
options.b: Company X has a higher break-even point than Company Y
options.c: Company Y is less likely than Company X to make a loss if sales fall
options.d: Company X's sales can fall much further than Company Y's before it starts making a loss

questions.explanation: The margin of safety shows how far sales can fall before the business makes a loss, so a larger margin means lower risk. Option B cannot be concluded because the margin depends on both actual sales and break-even sales, option C reverses the meaning, and option A cannot be concluded without the cost figures.

questions.question: The amount that each unit sold contributes towards covering fixed costs (and then towards profit) is called the:
questions.explanation: Contribution margin, CM = P - v, is what each unit adds towards covering fixed cost once its own variable cost has been met. Option C is the cost of one extra unit, option D is total cost divided by output, and option B is actual sales minus break-even sales.

questions.question: The cost of producing one additional unit of output is known as:
questions.explanation: Marginal cost, MC = change in TC / change in Q, is the extra cost of producing one more unit. Option B spreads total cost over all units, option C does not change with output at all, and option A is price minus variable cost per unit.

questions.question: Which of the following is a FIXED cost for a bakery?

options.a: Monthly rent on the bakery premises

questions.explanation: A fixed cost stays constant regardless of output, as rent does whether the bakery makes 100 or 10,000 loaves. Options B, C and D all rise with each loaf produced, so they are variable costs.

questions.question: Two cost plans are compared: one has a low fixed charge and a high cost per unit, the other a high fixed charge and a low cost per unit. BELOW their indifference point, which plan is cheaper?

options.a: The plan with the lower cost per unit
options.b: The plan with the lower fixed charge
options.c: Both plans cost exactly the same
options.d: It cannot be determined without the selling price

questions.explanation: Below the indifference point few units are involved, so the fixed charge dominates and the plan with the lower fixed charge is cheaper; above it, the lower cost per unit wins. Option A is only cheaper above the indifference point, option C is true only at that point, and option D is wrong because the comparison involves costs only.

questions.question: Break-even revenue (break-even sales in naira) is calculated as:

options.a: break-even quantity x variable cost per unit
options.b: fixed cost / selling price per unit
options.c: break-even quantity x selling price per unit
options.d: fixed cost x selling price per unit

questions.explanation: BER = BEQ x P converts the break-even number of units into naira sales. Option A gives the total variable cost at break-even, not revenue, option D has no meaning, and option B ignores variable cost and would understate break-even units.

questions.question: Which of the following expressions is equal to profit, where Q is quantity, P is price, v is variable cost per unit and FC is fixed cost?
questions.explanation: Profit = TR - TC = PQ - (FC + vQ) = Q(P - v) - FC, i.e. total contribution minus fixed cost. Option C adds fixed cost instead of subtracting it, option B is the break-even quantity, and option A forgets to multiply contribution by the number of units.

questions.question: In the formula Percentage Change = (New Value - Old Value) / Old Value x 100, the change is measured relative to:

options.a: the average of the old and new values
options.b: the sum of the old and new values

questions.explanation: Percentage change always divides the change by the original (old) value. Dividing by the new value, as in option C, is a common mistake that understates an increase, and options A and B are not part of the formula.

questions.question: A manager states that 'labour used must not exceed 100 hours per week'. Which mathematical form best expresses this?
questions.explanation: A limit that must not be exceeded is a constraint, written as a linear inequality using <= ; such inequalities are the constraints of linear programming. Option D forces labour to be exactly 100 hours, which is stricter than 'must not exceed', while options C and A are unrelated operations.

questions.question: A Lagos printing firm has fixed costs of N450,000 per month and a variable cost of N320 per copy. Using TC = FC + VQ, what is its total cost for a month in which it produces 2,500 copies?
questions.explanation: TC = FC + VQ = 450,000 + 320 x 2,500 = 450,000 + 800,000 = N1,250,000. Option B is only the variable cost and forgets the fixed cost, option C adds the cost of a single unit instead of 2,500 units, and option D wrongly multiplies the fixed and variable costs.

questions.question: A furniture maker in Aba sells 1,840 stools at N6,500 each. What is its total revenue?
questions.explanation: TR = P x Q = 6,500 x 1,840 = N11,960,000. Option C adds price and quantity instead of multiplying, while options A and B are place-value slips that are ten times too small or too large.

questions.question: A firm has fixed costs of N1,200,000, a selling price of N900 per unit and a variable cost of N540 per unit. What is its profit when it sells 5,000 units?
questions.explanation: Profit = Q(P - v) - FC = 5,000 x (900 - 540) - 1,200,000 = 1,800,000 - 1,200,000 = N600,000. Option D is total contribution and forgets the fixed cost, option A ignores variable cost, and option B adds the fixed cost instead of subtracting it.

questions.question: A water-packaging firm has fixed costs of N2,400,000, sells each bag pack at N1,500 and has a variable cost of N900 per pack. If market demand is only 3,000 packs, what is the result?
questions.explanation: Profit = Q(P - v) - FC = 3,000 x 600 - 2,400,000 = 1,800,000 - 2,400,000 = -600,000, a loss of N600,000, because 3,000 packs is below the break-even point of 4,000 packs. Option D gets the size right but the sign wrong, option B is the loss only at zero output, and option A is total contribution with fixed cost ignored.

questions.question: Chika's Kitchen has fixed costs of N840,000 per month. Each meal sells for N650 and has a variable cost of N440. What is the break-even point in meals per month?
questions.explanation: BEP = FC / (P - V) = 840,000 / (650 - 440) = 840,000 / 210 = 4,000 meals. Option C divides by price and ignores variable cost, option A divides by variable cost, and option D adds the variable cost to price instead of subtracting it.

questions.question: A cosmetics producer has fixed costs of N1,800,000, a selling price of N2,000 per jar and a variable cost of N1,250 per jar. What is its break-even revenue in naira?
questions.explanation: BEQ = 1,800,000 / (2,000 - 1,250) = 2,400 jars, so BER = BEQ x P = 2,400 x 2,000 = N4,800,000. Option B multiplies by variable cost instead of price, option A multiplies by contribution (which just gives back the fixed cost), and option D uses a formula with no meaning.

questions.question: Bisi Bags has fixed costs of N960,000, sells each bag for N1,200 and has a variable cost of N800 per bag. How many bags must it sell to earn a target profit of N640,000?
questions.explanation: Required units = (FC + Target Profit) / (P - V) = (960,000 + 640,000) / (1,200 - 800) = 1,600,000 / 400 = 4,000 bags. Option A forgets that fixed cost must be covered first, option B is just the break-even point, and option C divides by price instead of contribution.

questions.question: A firm has fixed costs of N1,500,000, a selling price of N750 and a variable cost of N450 per unit. It currently sells 7,200 units. What is its margin of safety in units?
questions.explanation: BEP = 1,500,000 / (750 - 450) = 5,000 units, so margin of safety = actual sales - break-even sales = 7,200 - 5,000 = 2,200 units. Option C is the break-even point itself, option D computes break-even by dividing by price, and option A adds instead of subtracting.

questions.question: A snack maker has fixed costs of N720,000, sells each pack for N400 and has a variable cost of N280 per pack. Budgeted sales are 8,500 packs. What is the margin of safety in naira (valued at selling price)?
questions.explanation: BEP = 720,000 / (400 - 280) = 6,000 packs; margin of safety = 8,500 - 6,000 = 2,500 packs, and in naira 2,500 x 400 = N1,000,000. Option C values the margin at variable cost, option B values it at contribution per unit, and option D is break-even revenue, not the margin of safety.

questions.question: A firm has fixed costs of N1,350,000, a selling price of N500 and a variable cost of N320 per unit, and actual sales of 9,000 units. Expressing the margin of safety as a percentage of ACTUAL sales, what is the margin of safety (to 1 decimal place)?
questions.explanation: BEP = 1,350,000 / (500 - 320) = 7,500 units; margin of safety = 9,000 - 7,500 = 1,500 units, and 1,500 / 9,000 x 100 = 16.7%. Option C divides by break-even sales instead of actual sales, option D is break-even sales as a share of actual sales, and option B is the contribution as a share of price.

questions.question: A cap maker has fixed costs of N600,000 and a variable cost of N350 per cap. It expects to sell exactly 4,000 caps. What selling price per cap would make it just break even?
questions.explanation: At break-even TR = TC, so P x 4,000 = 600,000 + 350 x 4,000; P = 350 + 600,000 / 4,000 = 350 + 150 = N500. Option C covers only fixed cost per cap, option D covers only variable cost, and option A doubles the fixed-cost share by mistake.

questions.question: A firm breaks even at 2,500 units. Its selling price is N1,800 per unit and its variable cost is N1,100 per unit. What are its fixed costs?
questions.explanation: Since BEP = FC / (P - V), FC = BEP x (P - V) = 2,500 x (1,800 - 1,100) = 2,500 x 700 = N1,750,000. Option A is break-even revenue, option C is total variable cost at break-even, and option D adds price and variable cost.

questions.question: A firm's fixed cost is N300,000 and its variable cost is N125 per unit. Using AC = TC / Q, what is its average cost per unit at an output of 2,000 units?
questions.explanation: TC = 300,000 + 125 x 2,000 = 550,000, so AC = 550,000 / 2,000 = N275. Option D is only the variable cost per unit, option A is only fixed cost per unit, and option B is total cost, which has not been divided by output.

questions.question: A factory's total cost is N1,240,000 when it produces 400 units and N1,330,000 when it produces 450 units. Using MC = change in TC / change in Q, what is the marginal cost per unit over this range?
questions.explanation: MC = (1,330,000 - 1,240,000) / (450 - 400) = 90,000 / 50 = N1,800 per unit. Options D and A are average costs at one output level, and option C is the total change in cost, not divided by the change in output.

questions.question: A firm's total cost follows a straight line TC = a + bx. Total cost is N650,000 at 1,000 units and N860,000 at 1,600 units. What is the variable cost per unit, b?
questions.explanation: b = (change in TC) / (change in units) = (860,000 - 650,000) / (1,600 - 1,000) = 210,000 / 600 = N350. Options C and D are average costs at one level, which wrongly include fixed cost, and option A is an average of the two totals, which also includes fixed cost.

questions.question: A delivery firm's monthly cost is linear, TC = a + bx, where x is the number of deliveries. TC is N380,000 for 200 deliveries and N590,000 for 500 deliveries. What is the fixed cost, a?
questions.explanation: First b = (590,000 - 380,000) / (500 - 200) = N700 per delivery; then a = TC - bx = 380,000 - 700 x 200 = N240,000. Option C is the variable cost per delivery, option B pairs the lower cost with the higher output, and option D is just the change in total cost.

questions.question: A trader in Onitsha buys a pair of shoes for N1,600 and sells it for N2,000. What is the mark-up percentage?
questions.explanation: Mark-up = (SP - Cost) / Cost x 100 = (2,000 - 1,600) / 1,600 x 100 = 400 / 1,600 x 100 = 25%. Option A is the margin, which divides by selling price, option D is cost as a share of selling price, and option B simply divides the profit by 100.

questions.question: A phone accessory costs N3,600 and is sold for N4,500. What is the margin on selling price?
questions.explanation: Margin = (SP - Cost) / SP x 100 = (4,500 - 3,600) / 4,500 x 100 = 900 / 4,500 x 100 = 20%. Option C is the mark-up on cost, which is always larger for a profitable item, option B is cost as a share of price, and option D is price as a share of cost.

questions.question: A bookshop prices its stock at a mark-up of 35% on cost. What is the selling price of a book that costs N2,400?
questions.explanation: SP = Cost x (1 + mark-up) = 2,400 x 1.35 = N3,240. Option A treats 35% as a margin on selling price, option C subtracts the mark-up, and option B adds 35 naira instead of 35%.

questions.question: A retailer wants a margin of 25% on SELLING PRICE for an item that costs her N3,000. What selling price should she charge?
questions.explanation: Margin is based on selling price, so Cost = SP x (1 - 0.25); SP = 3,000 / 0.75 = N4,000 (check: profit 1,000 / 4,000 = 25%). Option D applies 25% to cost, which is a mark-up and gives only a 20% margin, option C subtracts instead of adding, and option A doubles the percentage.

questions.question: A shirt is sold for N6,900, which includes a mark-up of 15% on cost. What did the shirt cost?
questions.explanation: SP = Cost x (1 + 0.15), so Cost = 6,900 / 1.15 = N6,000. Option C takes 15% off the selling price, which treats the mark-up as if it were based on selling price, option A divides by 1.5 instead of 1.15, and option D adds a further mark-up instead of removing it.

questions.question: An item is sold at a mark-up of 60% on cost. What is the equivalent margin on selling price?
questions.explanation: Take cost = 100; SP = 160, profit = 60, so margin = 60 / 160 x 100 = 37.5%. Option A assumes mark-up and margin are equal, option B subtracts from 100, and option D divides by 40, which is the formula for converting a margin into a mark-up.

questions.question: A supermarket earns a margin of 30% on the selling price of its goods. What is the equivalent mark-up on cost, to 2 decimal places?
questions.explanation: Take SP = 100; profit = 30, cost = 70, so mark-up = 30 / 70 x 100 = 42.86%. Option B assumes margin and mark-up are the same, option A divides by 130, which converts the other way round, and option C is just the cost share of price.

questions.question: A Lagos restaurant's monthly sales rose from N1,250,000 to N1,550,000. What is the percentage increase, to 1 decimal place?
questions.explanation: Percentage change = (New - Old) / Old x 100 = (1,550,000 - 1,250,000) / 1,250,000 x 100 = 300,000 / 1,250,000 x 100 = 24.0%. Option A divides by the new value, option B is the new value as a percentage of the old, and option C is a place-value slip.

questions.question: Production of cartons at a factory fell from 480 per day to 396 per day. What is the percentage change?
questions.explanation: Percentage change = (396 - 480) / 480 x 100 = -84 / 480 x 100 = -17.5%, a decrease of 17.5%. Option B divides by the new value, option C has the right size but the wrong direction, and option D is the new output as a percentage of the old.

questions.question: Two partners, Ade and Bola, share a profit of N960,000 in the ratio 3:5 respectively. How much does Bola receive?
questions.explanation: Total parts = 3 + 5 = 8; Bola's share = 5/8 x 960,000 = N600,000. Option C is Ade's share, option A wrongly divides by Ade's 3 parts instead of the total, and option B splits the profit equally.

questions.question: If 12 machine operators produce 1,500 units in a shift, how many units would 20 operators produce in a shift, assuming output is directly proportional to the number of operators?
questions.explanation: Output per operator = 1,500 / 12 = 125 units, so 20 operators produce 20 x 125 = 2,500 units. Option B inverts the proportion, option D adds the extra operators as if each were one unit, and option C forgets to divide by the original 12 operators.

questions.question: Using I = P x R x T, what is the simple interest on N450,000 invested for 3 years at 12% per annum?
questions.explanation: I = P x R x T = 450,000 x 0.12 x 3 = N162,000. Option B is the interest for only one year, option D is compound interest, and option C is the total amount (principal plus interest) rather than the interest.

questions.question: N380,000 is deposited at 7.5% per annum simple interest for 4 years. Using A = P(1 + RT), what is the amount at the end of the period?
questions.explanation: A = P(1 + RT) = 380,000 x (1 + 0.075 x 4) = 380,000 x 1.30 = N494,000. Option B is only the interest, option D uses the compound interest formula, and option C covers just one year.

questions.question: A loan of N250,000 attracts simple interest of N90,000 over 4 years. What is the annual rate of interest?
questions.explanation: From I = PRT, R = I / (P x T) = 90,000 / (250,000 x 4) = 0.09 = 9% per annum. Option D forgets to divide by the 4 years, option B forgets to convert the decimal to a percentage, and option A wrongly divides by principal plus interest.

questions.question: How many years will it take N400,000 to grow to N560,000 at 8% per annum simple interest?
questions.explanation: Interest needed = 560,000 - 400,000 = 160,000; T = I / (P x R) = 160,000 / (400,000 x 0.08) = 160,000 / 32,000 = 5 years. Option B uses the final amount instead of the interest, option D is the compound-interest answer, and option A bases the yearly interest on the final amount instead of the principal.

questions.question: Mrs Okafor invests N500,000 at 12% per annum compounded annually. Using A = P(1 + R)^n, what is the amount after 3 years, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: A = 500,000 x (1.12)^3 = 500,000 x 1.404928 = N702,464. Option A is the simple-interest amount, option B is only the compound interest earned, and option D compounds for one year too few.

questions.question: N800,000 is invested for 4 years at 9% per annum compounded annually. What is the compound interest EARNED, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: A = 800,000 x (1.09)^4 = 1,129,265.29, so interest earned = A - P = 1,129,265.29 - 800,000 = N329,265. Option C is the full amount rather than the interest, option A is simple interest, and option D subtracts the first year's amount instead of the principal.

questions.question: N600,000 is invested for 4 years at 10% per annum. By how much does the amount under annual compound interest exceed the amount under simple interest, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: Compound: 600,000 x (1.1)^4 = 878,460; simple: 600,000 x (1 + 0.1 x 4) = 840,000; difference = N38,460, the interest on interest. Option D is the simple interest itself, option A is the compound interest itself, and option B is just one year's simple interest.

questions.question: N200,000 is invested at 8% per annum compounded QUARTERLY for 2 years. Using A = P(1 + R)^n with R as the rate per quarter and n as the number of quarters, what is the amount, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: R per quarter = 8% / 4 = 2% and n = 4 x 2 = 8 quarters, so A = 200,000 x (1.02)^8 = N234,332. Option B compounds annually, option D uses the annual rate for every quarter, and option C uses the quarterly rate but only 2 periods.

questions.question: How much must a parent invest today at 10% per annum compounded annually to have N1,000,000 for school fees in 3 years' time? Give the answer to the nearest naira.
questions.explanation: From A = P(1 + R)^n, P = A / (1 + R)^n = 1,000,000 / (1.1)^3 = 1,000,000 / 1.331 = N751,315. Option B uses simple interest, option C reduces by 10% each year, which is not the same as dividing by 1.1, and option A grows the amount instead of discounting it.

questions.question: Solve for x: 5x - 18 = 2x + 27.
questions.explanation: Collect x terms on one side and numbers on the other: 5x - 2x = 27 + 18, so 3x = 45 and x = 15. Option D subtracts 18 instead of adding it, option B adds the x coefficients instead of subtracting, and option C ignores the 2x on the right-hand side.

questions.question: A sales agent earns a fixed weekly allowance of N15,000 plus N450 commission on every unit sold. Last week she earned N42,000 in total. How many units did she sell?
questions.explanation: Set up the equation 15,000 + 450x = 42,000; then 450x = 27,000 and x = 27,000 / 450 = 60 units. Option B ignores the fixed allowance, option A adds the allowance instead of subtracting it, and option D divides only the allowance by the commission.

questions.question: Data Plan A charges a fixed N1,000 per month plus N8 per megabyte; Data Plan B charges a fixed N3,500 per month plus N3 per megabyte. At how many megabytes per month do the two plans cost the same?
questions.explanation: Set the costs equal: 1,000 + 8m = 3,500 + 3m, so 5m = 2,500 and m = 500 MB. Option A adds the fixed fees instead of subtracting, option D adds the rates instead of subtracting, and option C ignores Plan A's fee and Plan B's rate.

questions.question: Courier X charges N8,000 plus N120 per km; Courier Y charges N20,000 plus N70 per km. For a 400 km delivery, which courier is cheaper and by how much?
questions.explanation: Cost X = 8,000 + 120 x 400 = N56,000; Cost Y = 20,000 + 70 x 400 = N48,000, so Y is cheaper by N8,000. This fits the indifference point of 12,000/50 = 240 km: beyond it the lower per-km rate wins. Option A picks the wrong courier, option C compares fixed charges only, and option B compares only the per-km charges and picks the wrong courier.

questions.question: A firm sells only cabinets at N15,000 each and stools at N6,000 each. Last month it sold 150 items in total for revenue of N1,530,000. How many cabinets did it sell?
questions.explanation: Let T = cabinets and S = stools: T + S = 150 and 15,000T + 6,000S = 1,530,000. Substituting S = 150 - T gives 15,000T + 900,000 - 6,000T = 1,530,000, so 9,000T = 630,000 and T = 70 (stools = 80). Option A is the number of stools, option C assumes all revenue came from cabinets, and option B simply halves the total.

questions.question: A caterer's orders give two equations for the price of a plate of rice (x) and a plate of beans (y), in naira: 2x + 3y = 3,100 and 4x + y = 3,200. What is the price of a plate of rice, x?
questions.explanation: Multiply the second equation by 3: 12x + 3y = 9,600; subtract the first: 10x = 6,500, so x = N650 (and y = N600). Check: 2(650) + 3(600) = 3,100. Option D is the value of y, option A ignores y in the second equation, and option B averages the totals over all coefficients.

questions.question: Each chair takes 4 hours of carpentry and only 150 carpentry hours are available per week, so 4x <= 150. What is the largest whole number of chairs, x, that can be made in a week?
questions.explanation: From 4x <= 150, x <= 37.5; since chairs must be whole and the limit cannot be exceeded, the maximum is 37. Option A rounds up and would need 152 hours, more than available, option D is not a whole number of chairs, and option B multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.question: A company's annual sales are N2,500,000 this year and are expected to grow at 8% per year compound. Using indices, what are the expected sales in 4 years' time, to the nearest naira?
questions.explanation: Sales = 2,500,000 x (1.08)^4 = 2,500,000 x 1.36048896 = N3,401,222. Option C adds 8% of the first year's sales each year (simple growth), option D uses one year too few, and option A compounds for one year too many.

questions.question: Using logarithms, how many complete years are needed for an investment to at least DOUBLE at 10% per annum compounded annually? (Solve (1.1)^n = 2.)
questions.explanation: Taking logs, n = log 2 / log 1.1 = 0.30103 / 0.04139 = 7.27, so the investment first doubles after 8 complete years. Option B rounds down, but after 7 years the factor is only 1.9487, option A is the simple-interest answer (10% x 10 = 100%), and option C is the exact solution of the equation, which is not a whole number of years.

questions.question: A company plans a circular water tank base with a radius of 14 m. Using Area = pi x r^2 with pi = 3.142, what is the area of the base?
questions.explanation: Area = 3.142 x 14^2 = 3.142 x 196 = 615.832 m^2. Option B is the circumference (2 x pi x r), option A forgets to square the radius, and option C squares the diameter instead of the radius.

questions.question: A cold room is 30 m long, 18 m wide and 6 m high. What is its storage volume?
questions.explanation: Volume = L x B x H = 30 x 18 x 6 = 3,240 m^3. Option A is only the floor area, option B is the total surface area of the room, and option D just adds the three dimensions.

questions.question: A firm sells 4,000 units at N1,000 each, with a variable cost of N600 per unit and fixed costs of N900,000. If it raises its price by 10% and sales volume stays the same, what will its new profit be?
questions.explanation: New price = 1,000 x 1.1 = 1,100; new profit = 4,000 x (1,100 - 600) - 900,000 = 2,000,000 - 900,000 = N1,100,000. Option D simply adds 10% to the old profit of N700,000, option B is the old profit, and option C forgets the fixed cost.

questions.question: A firm has fixed costs of N1,000,000, a selling price of N500 and a variable cost of N300 per unit. If fixed costs rise by 20% with price and variable cost unchanged, what is the new break-even point?
questions.explanation: New FC = 1,000,000 x 1.2 = 1,200,000; new BEP = 1,200,000 / (500 - 300) = 6,000 units, up from 5,000, because more fixed cost must be covered by the same contribution. Option B is the old break-even point, option C wrongly reduces it, and option D divides by price instead of contribution.

questions.question: A trader wants a total profit of N750,000 and makes a profit of N2,500 on each unit she sells. How many units must she sell?
questions.explanation: Units required = target profit / profit per unit = 750,000 / 2,500 = 300 units. Option D multiplies instead of dividing, option A wrongly subtracts one unit's profit first, and option C is a place-value slip.

questions.question: A bakery pays N250,000 a month in rent and salaries regardless of output, and spends N180 on ingredients and packaging for each loaf. Which function gives its total monthly cost (TC) for Q loaves?
questions.explanation: Total cost = fixed cost + (variable cost per unit x quantity), so TC = 250,000 + 180Q. Option B swaps the fixed and variable parts, option A makes fixed cost depend on output and subtracts the variable cost, and option D wrongly multiplies the fixed cost by output too.

questions.question: A firm expects to sell 5,000 units. Its fixed costs are N1,100,000 and its variable cost is N700 per unit. What selling price per unit will give it a profit of exactly N400,000?
questions.explanation: Profit = Q(P - v) - FC, so 400,000 = 5,000(P - 700) - 1,100,000; P = 700 + (1,100,000 + 400,000) / 5,000 = 700 + 300 = N1,000. Option B is only the break-even price, option A ignores fixed cost, and option C forgets to add the variable cost per unit.

questions.question: A factory's fixed costs are N3,600,000 per quarter and each unit sold contributes N1,440 towards fixed costs. How many units must it sell in the quarter to break even?
questions.explanation: BEQ = FC / contribution per unit = 3,600,000 / 1,440 = 2,500 units. Option D doubles the answer, option B inverts the division, and option C halves the answer; none of these makes total contribution equal fixed cost.

questions.question: Data collected first-hand by a researcher for a specific purpose is called:
questions.explanation: Primary data are collected first-hand by the researcher for the specific purpose at hand, for example through a questionnaire or interview. Secondary data (A) were collected by someone else for another purpose, while discrete (C) and grouped (D) describe the type or arrangement of data, not how they were collected.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of secondary data?

options.a: A questionnaire administered by the analyst
options.b: Government statistics published by the NBS

questions.explanation: Statistics published by the National Bureau of Statistics were collected by someone else for another purpose, so an analyst who reuses them is using secondary data. A questionnaire (A), an experiment (C) and direct observation (D) are all ways the analyst collects primary data personally.

questions.question: Discrete data can be described as:

options.a: Data that can take any value within a range

questions.explanation: Discrete data are countable and take whole-number values, such as the number of employees in a branch. Option A describes continuous data, option C mixes up the type of data with a collection method, and option D describes qualitative (categorical) data.

questions.question: Which chart is most appropriate for comparing sales across five different regions?
questions.explanation: A bar chart is the best choice for comparing separate categories such as regions, because the bar lengths can be compared directly. A pie chart (A) shows parts of a whole, a histogram (B) shows the distribution of a continuous variable, and a scatter diagram (D) shows the relationship between two variables.

questions.question: In a histogram, the bars:

options.b: Touch one another because the variable is continuous
options.d: Must all be the same colour

questions.explanation: Histogram bars are drawn touching each other because they represent continuous class intervals with no break between them. Gaps between bars (A) and categorical data (C) are features of a bar chart, and colour (D) has nothing to do with how a histogram is defined.

questions.question: The angle of a pie chart slice is calculated as:
questions.explanation: A full circle is 360 degrees, so each slice gets (value / total) x 360 degrees. Option A gives the percentage of the total, not the angle, and options C and D do not produce a share of the circle at all.

questions.question: A line graph is best suited to showing:
questions.explanation: A line graph joins data points over successive periods, so it is the standard chart for showing a trend over time, such as monthly revenue. Composition of a whole (A) suits a pie chart, a frequency distribution (C) suits a histogram, and a categorical comparison (D) suits a bar chart.

questions.question: The width of a class in a grouped frequency distribution is approximately:
questions.explanation: Class width is found by dividing the range (highest value minus lowest value) by the number of classes you want, then usually rounding up to a convenient figure. Option C turns the formula upside down, option A is a ratio rather than a range, and option D is the formula for a mean.

questions.question: Which of the following is a method of primary data collection?
questions.explanation: An interview collects information directly from respondents for the researcher's own purpose, so it is a primary method. Annual reports (A), NBS inflation data (C) and trade journals (D) already exist and were prepared by others, so using them means relying on secondary data.

questions.question: A pie chart is generally unsuitable when there are:

options.c: More than five or six categories

questions.explanation: With more than about five or six categories, a pie chart fills up with thin slices that are hard to read and compare, so a bar chart is usually better. Two or three categories (A and B) are well within what a pie chart handles comfortably.

questions.question: Continuous data differs from discrete data in that continuous data:

options.b: Can take any value within a given range

questions.explanation: Continuous data can take any value within a range, including fractions, such as weight or time. Whole-number values only (A) describe discrete data, continuous data are measured rather than unmeasurable (C), and categorical data (D) are qualitative.

questions.question: Class boundaries for whole-number data are typically obtained by:

options.b: Adding and subtracting 0.5 from the class limits
options.c: Dividing class limits by the number of classes

questions.explanation: For whole-number data, class boundaries are found by subtracting 0.5 from the lower limit and adding 0.5 to the upper limit, so that 38-42 becomes 37.5-42.5 and there are no gaps between classes. Multiplying (A) or dividing (C) the limits does not close the gaps between classes.

questions.question: A firm's marketing team designs and administers its own customer satisfaction survey. The data it collects are best described as:
questions.explanation: The team collected the information first-hand for its own specific purpose, so the survey results are primary data. Secondary data (A), existing records (D) and published data (C) all refer to information that someone else has already collected for another purpose.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes secondary data?

options.a: Data collected first-hand by the researcher for a specific purpose
options.b: Data that can only take whole-number values
options.c: Data already collected by someone else for another purpose and reused by the analyst
options.d: Data obtained by changing one variable under controlled conditions

questions.explanation: Secondary data already exist because someone else collected them for a different purpose, such as NBS inflation statistics, and the analyst simply reuses them. Option A describes primary data, option B describes discrete data, and option D describes an experiment, which is a primary method.

questions.question: Which list contains ONLY methods of primary data collection?
questions.explanation: Questionnaires, interviews and observation all gather fresh data directly for the researcher, as do experiments. Each of the other lists includes a secondary item: NBS statistics in B, annual reports and trade journals in D, and published financial statements in C.

questions.question: A company changes one ingredient in a product formula under controlled conditions and records the effect on taste ratings. Which data collection method is this?
questions.explanation: An experiment deliberately changes one variable under controlled conditions to see its effect, which is what testing a new formula does. Observation (A) records behaviour as it happens without manipulating anything, while interviews (B) and questionnaires (C) ask people questions.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of continuous data?

options.a: The number of customers served per day
options.b: The number of staff in a branch
options.c: The weight of bags of rice in kilograms
options.d: The number of cars sold in a month

questions.explanation: Weight can take any value within a range, such as 49.75 kg, so it is continuous data. The number of staff (B), customers (A) and cars (D) are all counts that take whole-number values, which makes them discrete data.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a histogram from a bar chart?

options.a: A bar chart's bars touch and show a continuous variable, while a histogram's bars are separated and compare categories
options.b: Both have gaps between bars; they differ only in colour
options.c: A histogram's bars touch and show the distribution of a continuous variable, while a bar chart's bars are separated and compare categories
options.d: In a bar chart bar area shows frequency, while in a histogram only bar height matters

questions.explanation: A histogram shows how one continuous variable is distributed across numerical classes, so its bars touch, while a bar chart compares separate categories with gaps between bars. Option A reverses the two, option B ignores the real difference, and option D also reverses them, since it is in a histogram that bar area represents frequency.

questions.question: In a histogram, the frequency of each class is represented by:
questions.explanation: In a histogram the area of each bar is proportional to the frequency of its class, which matters especially when classes have unequal widths. Histograms have no gaps between bars (A), colour carries no frequency information (B), and slice angles (C) belong to pie charts.

questions.question: Why would a pie chart be unsuitable for presenting data with 12 categories?

options.a: A pie chart cannot show angles greater than 180 degrees
options.b: Many thin slices clutter the chart and make similar-sized slices hard to compare
options.c: A pie chart can only show trends over time
options.d: A pie chart can only be used for continuous data

questions.explanation: Pie charts work best with about five or six categories or fewer; with 12, the slices become thin and similar slices are hard to tell apart. A pie chart uses the full 360 degrees (A), trends over time suit a line graph (C), and pie charts show parts of a whole, not continuous distributions (D).

questions.question: Which chart would usually present the values of 12 separate categories more clearly than a pie chart?
questions.explanation: A bar chart lets the reader compare 12 separate categories easily, because bar lengths are simple to line up and compare. A histogram (D) is for continuous grouped data, a scatter diagram (B) shows the relationship between two variables, and extra colours (C) do not solve the problem of too many thin slices.

questions.question: In a grouped frequency distribution, class width refers to:

options.c: The number of observations in a class
options.d: The size of each class interval

questions.explanation: Class width is the size of each class interval, estimated as (highest value - lowest value) / number of classes. The number of observations in a class (C) is its frequency, the midpoint (B) is the class mark, and the number of classes (A) is a separate choice made before finding the width.

questions.question: A data set has a highest value of 87 and a lowest value of 12. Using class width = (highest - lowest) / number of classes, what is the class width for 5 classes?
questions.explanation: The range is 87 - 12 = 75, and 75 / 5 = 15. Option D divides the highest value alone by 5, option C is the range before dividing, and option B divides the lowest value by 5.

questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of a well-constructed statistical table?

options.a: Leaving out totals even where they help the reader

questions.explanation: A good table has a clear title, labelled rows and columns with units stated, totals where appropriate, and a statement of where any secondary data came from. Unlabelled columns (D), missing units (C) and leaving out helpful totals (A) all make a table harder to understand.

questions.question: A line graph should be preferred over a bar chart when the aim is to:

options.a: Compare the sales of separate branches at one point in time
options.b: Compare the number of staff in different departments
options.c: Show how a variable changes over successive time periods
options.d: Show how a total budget is split into parts

questions.explanation: A line graph is the chart of choice when the message is a trend, because it joins values across successive periods. Comparing branches (A) or departments (B) at one point in time is a categorical comparison that suits a bar chart, and showing parts of a total (D) suits a pie chart.

questions.question: The monthly expenditure (N'000) of 24 households is: 35, 42, 28, 51, 39, 47, 33, 55, 44, 38, 49, 31, 46, 40, 53, 36, 48, 29, 50, 37, 45, 32, 41, 43. Using 6 classes, with class width = range / number of classes rounded UP to a whole number, what are the range and class width?
questions.explanation: The highest value is 55 and the lowest is 28, so the range is 27; 27 / 6 = 4.5, which rounds up to a class width of 5. Option A uses the highest value instead of the range, option C rounds down, which would leave some values outside the classes, and option B adds the highest and lowest values instead of subtracting them.

questions.question: The monthly expenditure (N'000) of 24 households is: 35, 42, 28, 51, 39, 47, 33, 55, 44, 38, 49, 31, 46, 40, 53, 36, 48, 29, 50, 37, 45, 32, 41, 43. Using the classes 28-32, 33-37, 38-42, 43-47, 48-52 and 53-57, what is the frequency of the class 38-42?
questions.explanation: The values falling in 38-42 are 38, 39, 40, 41 and 42, giving a frequency of 5. The full set of frequencies is 4, 4, 5, 5, 4 and 2, which correctly add up to 24; option D matches the neighbouring classes 28-32 and 33-37, not 38-42.

questions.question: A budget of N10,000,000 includes Raw Materials of N2,800,000. Using angle = (value / total) x 360 degrees, what is the pie-chart angle for Raw Materials?
questions.explanation: Raw Materials are 2,800,000 / 10,000,000 = 28% of the budget, and 0.28 x 360 = 100.8 degrees. Option B gives the percentage instead of the angle, while D (126 degrees) would be the angle for a 35% share and C (36 degrees) for a 10% share.

questions.question: A N10,000,000 budget is split as: Salaries N3,500,000; Raw Materials N2,800,000; Marketing N1,200,000; Overheads N1,500,000; Logistics N1,000,000. Which category would have a pie-chart angle of 54 degrees?
questions.explanation: An angle of 54 degrees is 54 / 360 = 15% of the total, which is N1,500,000, the Overheads figure. Marketing (C) at 12% gets 43.2 degrees, Logistics (A) at 10% gets 36 degrees, and Salaries (D) at 35% gets 126 degrees.

questions.question: A managing director wants to compare the performance of five branch managers this quarter. Which chart is most suitable?
questions.explanation: Five branch managers are separate categories being compared at one point in time, which is exactly what a bar chart is for. A pie chart (C) shows parts of a whole, a line graph (D) shows a trend over time, and a histogram (A) shows the distribution of a continuous variable.

questions.question: A managing director wants to see the distribution of the ages of 150 employees. Which chart is most suitable?
questions.explanation: Age is a continuous variable, and showing how 150 ages are spread across age classes is a frequency distribution, which a histogram presents. A pie chart (B) shows shares of a total, a line graph (C) shows change over time, and a scatter diagram (A) shows the relationship between two variables.

questions.question: A managing director wants to see how the company's monthly profit has changed over the past two years. Which chart is most suitable?
questions.explanation: Monthly profit over two years is a trend over successive time periods, which a line graph shows best. A pie chart (C) shows composition of a whole, a histogram (A) shows a frequency distribution, and an organisational chart (D) shows reporting relationships, not figures.

questions.question: Compared with tables, a major limitation of charts and graphs when reporting to senior management is that they:

options.a: Take longer to interpret at a glance
options.b: May lose precision and can be made misleading, for example through distorted scales
options.d: Always preserve exact figures better than tables

questions.explanation: Charts communicate patterns quickly, but readers cannot easily see exact figures, and a stretched or cut-off scale can mislead. Charts are actually faster to read at a glance (A), they are very good at showing comparisons (C), and it is tables, not charts, that preserve exact figures (D).

questions.question: What is the main advantage of presenting data in a table rather than a chart?

options.a: A table is always more persuasive to a busy audience
options.b: A table needs no title or labels
options.c: A table shows patterns and trends faster at a glance
options.d: A table preserves exact figures for detailed checking and verification

questions.explanation: Tables keep the precise values, which makes them useful for detailed checking and audit. Seeing patterns quickly (C) and persuading a busy audience (A) are strengths of charts, and a good table still needs a clear title and labels (B).

questions.question: Which of the following is a typical drawback of secondary data compared with primary data?

options.a: It may be outdated or collected for a different purpose
options.b: It cannot be obtained from government publications
options.c: It is always tailored to the specific research question
options.d: It is usually more expensive and slower to obtain

questions.explanation: Because secondary data were gathered by others for their own purposes, they may be out of date, defined differently or of uncertain quality for the current study. Secondary data are usually cheaper and faster to obtain (D), tailoring to the research question is a strength of primary data (C), and government publications such as NBS statistics are a common place to find secondary data (B).

questions.question: Which of the following is a typical drawback of primary data?

options.a: It was collected by someone else for another purpose
options.b: It is usually out of date
options.c: It is more costly and time-consuming to collect
options.d: It is not tailored to the specific research question

questions.explanation: Collecting fresh data through surveys, interviews or experiments takes time and money, which is the main drawback of primary data. Options D, B and A describe weaknesses of secondary data, because primary data are collected now, for the specific purpose, by the researcher.

questions.question: Published reports, government statistics, and past research are examples of:
questions.explanation: Published reports, government statistics and past research were collected by other people for their own purposes, which makes them secondary data, so D is correct. Option C, primary data, is collected first-hand for your own purpose. Options A and B describe the nature of data (non-numerical, or named categories), not who collected it.

questions.question: Which of these is a characteristic of qualitative data collection?

options.a: Participants may be randomly assigned to treatments
options.b: Intent is to generalise findings to a larger population
options.c: Uses probability sampling to select participants
options.d: Open-ended and less structured in protocol

questions.explanation: Qualitative data collection is open-ended and less structured, letting participants explain context, meaning and experiences in their own words, so D is correct. Options A, B and C all describe quantitative research, which uses probability sampling, aims to generalise to a larger population and may randomly assign participants to treatments.

questions.question: Which sampling approach is typically used in qualitative research?
questions.explanation: Qualitative research picks participants deliberately because they can provide rich information on the topic, which is purposive or theoretical sampling, so D is correct. Options B and C are probability-based methods used when the goal is to generalise to a population, and option A is a feature of experiments, not a way of selecting people to study.

questions.question: Which chart is like a bar chart for continuous data, with no gaps between bars?
questions.explanation: A histogram shows the frequency distribution of continuous data, with bars standing side by side and no gaps because the class intervals run on continuously, so A is correct. Option B, the bar chart, compares separate categories and normally has gaps between bars. Option C is a cumulative frequency curve and option D shows parts of a whole.

questions.question: Which chart shows proportions by giving each category an angle = (frequency / total) x 360 degrees?
questions.explanation: A pie chart divides a full circle of 360 degrees into slices, with each slice's angle proportional to its share of the total, so B is correct. Option A plots pairs of values, option C shows change over time and option D shows the frequency distribution of continuous data, so none of them uses angles.

questions.question: Which tool is the basis for correlation and regression analysis?
questions.explanation: A scatter diagram plots pairs of values for two variables, letting you see whether and how closely they move together, which is why it is the starting point for correlation and regression; B is correct. Option A shows cumulative frequencies, option C compares categories and option D organises a single variable into classes, so none of them shows the relationship between two variables.

questions.question: A cumulative frequency curve used to find the median/quartiles graphically is called a(n):
questions.explanation: An ogive plots cumulative frequency against the class boundaries, and reading across at half the total frequency gives the median (at a quarter and three-quarters, the quartiles), so B is correct. Option A shows trends over time, option C shows parts of a whole and option D shows ordinary, not cumulative, frequencies.

questions.question: Extended one-on-one conversations used to uncover deep insights describe:
questions.explanation: In-depth interviews are long, one-on-one conversations designed to explore a person's views and experiences in detail, so A is correct. Option C involves watching behaviour rather than talking, option B means studying existing documents, and option D uses fixed answer choices that cannot uncover deep insights.

questions.question: Using multiple data collection methods together to strengthen findings is called:
questions.explanation: Triangulation means using more than one method or type of data to study the same question, so that findings confirmed in several ways are more credible; B is correct. Option A refers to assigning participants by chance, option C means keeping procedures the same for everyone, and option D means dividing a population into subgroups before sampling.

questions.question: The process of measuring and gathering information and variables in an established, systematic fashion that enables one to answer stated hypotheses and evaluate actions is called:
questions.explanation: Data collection is the systematic measuring and gathering of information so that stated hypotheses can be answered and actions evaluated. Option B comes later and shows the data in charts and tables, option C is arranging data in rows and columns, and option D is drawing meaning from data that have already been gathered.

questions.question: A supermarket manager in Ikeja designs her own questionnaire and gives it to 200 shoppers to measure their satisfaction with a new loyalty card. The data she obtains are:
questions.explanation: Primary data are collected first-hand by the researcher for a specific purpose, exactly as the manager does with her own questionnaire. Options D, B and C all describe data already collected by someone else for another purpose and then reused.

questions.question: A financial analyst uses exchange-rate figures published by the Central Bank of Nigeria to study how import costs have changed over five years. These figures are an example of:
questions.explanation: Secondary data were collected by someone else for another purpose and are reused by the analyst, as with published central bank statistics. Option B would require the analyst to collect the figures first-hand, while options A and C are primary methods in which the researcher runs an experiment or watches events directly.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a method of collecting primary data?

options.a: Extracting figures from a company's published financial statements
options.c: Observing customer flow in a store
options.d: Running a controlled experiment on a new product formula

questions.explanation: Extracting figures from published financial statements reuses data prepared by someone else, so it is a documentary (secondary) method. Options B, C and D (questionnaire, observation and experiment) all gather data first-hand for the researcher's own purpose.

questions.question: To study how shoppers move through a new store layout, a researcher stands quietly and records the paths customers take, without asking them any questions. Which data collection method is this?
questions.explanation: Observation records behaviour or events as they happen without questioning the subjects, which is how customer flow in a store is typically studied. Options B and D both involve asking people questions, and option C requires deliberately changing a variable under controlled conditions.

questions.question: A drinks company sells a new reduced-sugar formula in five outlets and the old formula in five similar outlets, keeping price and display the same, to see the effect on sales. This method of data collection is:
questions.explanation: An experiment manipulates one variable (here the formula) under controlled conditions to observe its effect, as when testing a new product formula. Option A only watches events without changing anything, option B questions people directly, and option D uses existing records.

questions.question: A structured set of written questions administered to respondents, commonly used for customer satisfaction surveys, is called:
questions.explanation: A questionnaire is a structured set of written questions given to respondents, which makes it well suited to customer satisfaction surveys. Option A is direct verbal questioning, option B records behaviour without questions, and option D manipulates a variable under controlled conditions.

questions.question: As a method of data collection, an interview is best described as:

options.a: extracting data from existing records or publications
options.b: a set of written questions that respondents complete on their own
options.c: direct verbal questioning, which may be structured or unstructured
options.d: recording events as they occur without asking any questions

questions.explanation: An interview gathers data through direct verbal questioning, structured or unstructured, and is often used for in-depth market research. Option B describes a questionnaire, option D describes observation, and option A describes the documentary (secondary) method.

questions.question: The number of customers served per day at a bank branch is an example of:
questions.explanation: Customers are counted in whole numbers (you cannot serve 12.6 customers), so the data are discrete quantitative data. Option B would apply to measurements such as time or weight that can take any value in a range, and options D and C describe categories or attributes rather than amounts.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of CONTINUOUS data?

options.a: The number of cars sold per week
options.b: The time taken to serve each customer at a fast-food counter
options.c: The number of staff in each branch
options.d: The brand of phone each customer prefers

questions.explanation: Continuous data can take any value within a range, and time can be measured to any fraction of a second. Options C and A are counts, which are discrete, and option D is a category, which is qualitative data.

questions.question: A market researcher records whether each respondent prefers Brand X, Brand Y or Brand Z of noodles. The variable 'brand preference' is:
questions.explanation: Brand preference describes a category or attribute rather than an amount, so it is qualitative (categorical) data. Options C and A are quantitative data that answer 'how much' or 'how many', and option B also refers to numerical measurement, which brand names are not.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT quantitative data?

options.a: The department each employee works in
options.b: Weight of each bag of rice produced
options.c: Number of employees in each branch

questions.explanation: The department is an attribute or category, so it is qualitative data. Options D, C and B answer 'how much' or 'how many' and are therefore quantitative (salary and weight are continuous, the number of employees is discrete).

questions.question: The main focus of QUANTITATIVE data collection is:

options.a: producing findings that are not meant to apply beyond the people studied
options.b: understanding context, processes, perspectives and meaning
options.c: testing hypotheses derived from theory and estimating the size of a phenomenon
options.d: selecting participants purposively to explore deep insights

questions.explanation: Quantitative data collection focuses on testing hypotheses derived from theory and estimating how large a phenomenon is. Options B, D and A all describe qualitative data collection, which seeks context and meaning, uses purposive sampling and does not aim to generalise.

questions.question: Which statement about generalisability is CORRECT?

options.a: Qualitative studies intend to generalise findings to a larger population, while quantitative findings are generally not generalisable
options.b: Quantitative studies intend to generalise findings to a larger population, while qualitative findings are generally not generalisable
options.c: Neither quantitative nor qualitative studies can say anything about a population
options.d: Both quantitative and qualitative studies always generalise their findings to the whole population

questions.explanation: Quantitative data collection aims to generalise its findings to a larger population, whereas qualitative findings are generally not generalisable to a specific population. Option A reverses the two approaches, option D ignores the difference between them, and option C is wrong because quantitative studies are designed to generalise.

questions.question: A researcher wants findings from a survey of Lagos SMEs to apply to ALL SMEs in Lagos. How should she select participants?

options.c: By choosing only firms she already knows well

questions.explanation: Quantitative research that aims to generalise to a population selects participants by probability sampling, so every unit has a known chance of selection. Options B and A are used in qualitative research, whose findings are not meant to be generalised, and option C is a convenience choice that would bias the results.

questions.question: A sampling method in which every member of the population has an equal chance of being selected, for example by drawing names from a hat, is:
questions.explanation: In simple random sampling every member of the population has an equal chance of selection, as in a lottery draw. Option B first divides the population into subgroups, option A picks every kth item from a list after a starting point, and option C deliberately chooses particular participants, so chances are not equal.

questions.question: A bank divides its staff into junior, senior and management groups and then selects a random sample from EACH group. This is:
questions.explanation: Stratified sampling divides the population into subgroups (strata) and draws a random sample from each, so every group is represented. Option C takes every kth name from a single list, option A samples from the whole population without forming groups, and option D is a non-probability method used in qualitative research.

questions.question: From an alphabetical list of 2,000 customers, a researcher picks the 5th name and then every 40th name after it. This is:
questions.explanation: Systematic sampling selects every kth item from an ordered list after a starting point, here every 40th customer after the 5th. Option A would first divide customers into subgroups, while options D and C are non-probability methods in which the researcher chooses participants deliberately.

questions.question: A frequency distribution is best described as:

options.a: a chart in which slices of a circle represent parts of a whole
options.b: a graph of points joined by lines to show change over time
options.c: a list of raw data in the exact order in which they were collected
options.d: an arrangement of raw data into classes showing the number of observations falling into each class

questions.explanation: A frequency distribution organises raw data into classes (or categories) and shows how many observations fall into each, which makes patterns easier to see. Option A describes a pie chart, option C is ungrouped raw data, which is what the distribution is meant to replace, and option B describes a line graph.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT true of a bar chart?

options.a: The lengths of its bars are proportional to the values they represent
options.b: Its bars are of equal width
options.c: Its bars touch each other because the variable is continuous
options.d: It is suitable for comparing discrete categories such as sales by region

questions.explanation: Bars that touch because the variable is continuous describe a histogram; a bar chart's bars are separated by gaps because the categories are separate. Options B, A and D are all true of a bar chart: equal-width bars, lengths proportional to values, and use for comparing discrete categories.

questions.question: The finance director of a Lagos firm wants to show the board how the total operating cost is split between salaries, rent, marketing and logistics. Which chart is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: A pie chart shows the composition of a whole, with each slice in proportion to its share of the total, and it works best with a few categories like these four. Option A is for trends over time, option C is for the distribution of a continuous grouped variable, and option D shows the relationship between two variables.

questions.question: An analyst wants to show how the naira-dollar exchange rate moved month by month over the last 24 months. Which chart should she use?
questions.explanation: A line graph joins data points with lines and is the standard chart for showing how a quantity changes over a continuous period, so it is the choice whenever the message is a trend. Option A shows parts of a whole, option D compares separate categories, and option B shows the distribution of grouped data rather than change over time.

questions.question: A delivery company has grouped the delivery times (in minutes) of 300 orders into classes such as 10-under 20, 20-under 30 and so on. To show the distribution of these times, the most appropriate chart is a:

options.b: Simple bar chart with gaps between bars

questions.explanation: A histogram is used for continuous, grouped quantitative data, with adjoining bars whose areas represent class frequencies, which fits grouped delivery times. Option A shows parts of a whole, option D shows a trend over time, and option B is for separate categories, not continuous classes.

questions.question: In a histogram, which feature of each bar is proportional to the frequency of its class?

options.c: Its position on the vertical axis label
options.d: The gap between it and the next bar

questions.explanation: In a histogram the area of each bar is proportional to the frequency of its class; when all classes have the same width, the heights also follow the frequencies. Option A carries no numerical meaning, option D is wrong because histogram bars have no gaps, and option C is not a feature of the bar itself.

questions.question: A marketing manager plots each month's advertising spend against that month's sales as a set of points, to see whether the two variables are related. This chart is a:
questions.explanation: A scatter diagram plots pairs of values to show the relationship between two variables and forms the basis for correlation and regression. Option B plots cumulative frequency, option C shows parts of a whole, and option D shows the distribution of one grouped variable.

questions.question: A 'less than' ogive is drawn by plotting:

options.a: cumulative frequencies against the lower class limits of the first class only
options.b: cumulative frequencies against the upper class boundaries
options.c: class frequencies against the class midpoints
options.d: percentages of the total against slice angles

questions.explanation: An ogive is a cumulative frequency curve; for a 'less than' ogive each cumulative frequency is plotted against the upper class boundary, because it counts all observations below that boundary. Option C describes a frequency polygon, option A would give only one point, and option D relates to a pie chart.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of a well-constructed statistical table?

options.c: Leaving out the units so the table looks less cluttered

questions.explanation: A good table states its units clearly; leaving them out makes the figures impossible to interpret correctly. Options A, D and B (a clear title, labelled rows and columns, and totals where appropriate) are all features of a good table, along with a statement of where secondary data came from.

questions.question: When is a table usually preferred to a chart for presenting data?

options.a: When the message is a trend over time
options.b: When the audience needs to see a pattern quickly without reading figures
options.c: When exact values matter more than visual impression
options.d: When the aim is to show parts of a whole at a glance

questions.explanation: Well-designed tables are one of the most precise ways to present data, so they are preferred when exact values matter more than visual impression. Options A, D and B are situations where charts (a line graph, a pie chart, or charts generally) communicate better because they show patterns at a glance.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a bar chart from a histogram?

options.a: There is no difference; the two names refer to the same chart
options.b: A bar chart compares separate categories and has gaps between bars; a histogram shows the distribution of a continuous variable and its bars touch
options.c: A bar chart's bars touch; a histogram's bars are separated by gaps
options.d: A bar chart shows the distribution of a continuous variable; a histogram compares separate categories

questions.explanation: A bar chart compares separate categories, so its bars are separated by gaps, while a histogram shows how one continuous variable is spread across numerical classes, so its bars touch. Options D and C reverse the two charts, and option A ignores a distinction that is often tested.

questions.question: An analyst studying inflation in Nigeria uses consumer price figures published by the National Bureau of Statistics. Which data collection method is she using?
questions.explanation: Extracting data from existing records or publications, such as NBS inflation statistics, is the documentary or secondary method. Options C, B and D are primary methods in which the analyst would gather new data herself.

questions.question: For whole-number data, the class 20-29 has 19.5 and 29.5 as its:
questions.explanation: Class boundaries for whole-number data are found by subtracting 0.5 from the lower limit and adding 0.5 to the upper limit, giving 19.5 and 29.5. Option D gives the stated values 20 and 29, option A would be the single value 24.5, and option B refers to counts of observations, not class edges.

questions.question: The daily sales (in N'000) of 16 kiosks are: 34, 47, 52, 41, 38, 49, 55, 44, 60, 39, 46, 51, 43, 58, 40, 36. What is the range of the data?
questions.explanation: Range = highest value - lowest value = 60 - 34 = 26. Option A is just the highest value, option C adds the extremes instead of subtracting, and option D is the mean, which is a measure of average, not spread.

questions.question: The daily sales (in N'000) of 16 kiosks are: 34, 47, 52, 41, 38, 49, 55, 44, 60, 39, 46, 51, 43, 58, 40, 36. In a grouped frequency distribution using classes 30-39, 40-49, 50-59 and 60-69, what is the frequency of the class 40-49?
questions.explanation: Tallying values from 40 to 49 inclusive gives [40, 41, 43, 44, 46, 47, 49], so the frequency is 7. Option C usually comes from leaving out the boundary value 40, option A from also counting a value outside the class, and option D is the frequency of class 50-59.

questions.question: A set of exam scores has a highest value of 97 and a lowest value of 42. Using Class Width = (Highest - Lowest) / Number of classes, rounded UP to the next whole number, what class width should be used for 6 classes?
questions.explanation: Class width = (97 - 42) / 6 = 55 / 6 = 9.17, rounded up to 10. Option B rounds down, which leaves the classes too narrow to cover the highest value, option A divides only the highest value, and option C adds the extremes instead of subtracting.

questions.question: For whole-number data, what are the class boundaries of the class 25-34?
questions.explanation: Class boundaries = class limits -/+ 0.5, so the lower boundary is 25 - 0.5 = 24.5 and the upper boundary is 34 + 0.5 = 34.5. Option B gives the class limits themselves, option C moves the boundaries inward instead of outward, and option D moves them out by a whole unit.

questions.question: What is the class midpoint (class mark) of the class 25-34?
questions.explanation: Class midpoint = (lower limit + upper limit) / 2 = (25 + 34) / 2 = 29.5, which is the same as (24.5 + 34.5) / 2. Option D uses 35 as the upper limit, option A is the difference between the limits, and option C adds the limits but forgets to divide by 2.

questions.question: A grouped frequency distribution of whole-number data uses the classes 10-19, 20-29, 30-39 and so on. Taking class width as upper class boundary minus lower class boundary, what is the class width?
questions.explanation: For 10-19 the boundaries are 9.5 and 19.5, so the width is 19.5 - 9.5 = 10 (also the gap between successive lower limits, 20 - 10). Option B subtracts the class limits (19 - 10), a common mistake, option A mixes a limit with a boundary, and option C is just the upper limit.

questions.question: In a survey of 40 traders, 15 fall in the turnover class N50,000-N99,999. What is the relative frequency of this class, as a percentage?
questions.explanation: Relative frequency = class frequency / total frequency x 100 = 15 / 40 x 100 = 37.5%. Option D divides by the traders outside the class, option A is the share of traders outside the class, and option C inverts the fraction.

questions.question: The marks of 40 staff in a training test are grouped as follows (class: frequency): 10-19: 4; 20-29: 9; 30-39: 15; 40-49: 8; 50-59: 4. What is the cumulative frequency up to and including the class 30-39?
questions.explanation: Cumulative frequency adds the frequencies up to that class: 4 + 9 + 15 = 28. Option A is only the frequency of 30-39, option B stops one class early, and option C goes one class too far.

questions.question: The marks of 40 staff are grouped as follows (class: frequency): 10-19: 4; 20-29: 9; 30-39: 15; 40-49: 8; 50-59: 4. On a 'less than' ogive, plotting cumulative frequency against upper class boundaries, which point is plotted for the class 30-39?
questions.explanation: The upper class boundary of 30-39 is 39 + 0.5 = 39.5 and the cumulative frequency to that point is 4 + 9 + 15 = 28, so the point is (39.5, 28). Option A uses the upper limit and the simple frequency, option B uses the class midpoint, and option D uses the lower boundary.

questions.question: The marks of 40 staff are grouped as follows (class: frequency): 10-19: 4; 20-29: 9; 30-39: 15; 40-49: 8; 50-59: 4. What percentage of the staff scored 40 marks or more?
questions.explanation: Staff scoring 40 or more are in 40-49 and 50-59: 8 + 4 = 12, and 12 / 40 x 100 = 30.0%. Option B counts only the 40-49 class, option A is the percentage BELOW 40, and option C wrongly includes the 30-39 class.

questions.question: Using these grouped marks (class: frequency): 10-19: 4; 20-29: 9; 30-39: 15; 40-49: 8; 50-59: 4, how many staff scored at least 30 marks?
questions.explanation: At least 30 means the classes 30-39, 40-49 and 50-59: 15 + 8 + 4 = 27. Option D is the cumulative frequency up to 39, which counts the wrong end of the table, option C is only the 30-39 class, and option B leaves out the 30-39 class.

questions.question: A firm's operating budget of N6,000,000 includes N1,350,000 for transport. Using Angle = (Value / Total) x 360 degrees, what angle should the transport slice have on a pie chart?
questions.explanation: Angle = (1,350,000 / 6,000,000) x 360 = 0.225 x 360 = 81.0 degrees. Option D is the percentage share (22.5%), not the angle, option B uses 180 instead of 360, and option C divides by the other categories instead of the whole budget.

questions.question: On a pie chart of a company's total sales of N5,000,000, the slice for Abuja has an angle of 72 degrees. What were Abuja's sales?
questions.explanation: Value = (angle / 360) x total = (72 / 360) x 5,000,000 = 0.2 x 5,000,000 = N1,000,000. Option C treats the angle as a percentage, option A divides the total by the angle, and option B uses 180 instead of 360.

questions.question: In a pie chart of staff by department, the Marketing slice has an angle of 54 degrees. What percentage of the staff work in Marketing?
questions.explanation: Percentage = angle / 360 x 100 = 54 / 360 x 100 = 15%. Option D reads the angle as a percentage, option A divides by 180 instead of 360, and option C is the share of all the other departments.

questions.question: A pie chart has five slices. Four of them have angles of 100, 120, 60, 45 degrees. What is the angle of the fifth slice?
questions.explanation: All slices of a pie chart must add up to 360 degrees, so the fifth slice = 360 - (100 + 120 + 60 + 45) = 360 - 325 = 35 degrees. Option C mixes degrees and percentages, option B assumes all five slices are equal (360 / 5), and option A doubles the correct figure.

questions.question: In a survey of 240 UNILAG students, 50 said they prefer a particular mobile network. What angle should this group have on a pie chart?
questions.explanation: Angle = (50 / 240) x 360 = 75 degrees. Option D is the percentage share, not the angle, option A arranges the formula wrongly, and option B uses 180 instead of 360.

questions.question: A budget of N10,000,000 gives N3,500,000 to salaries and N2,000,000 to marketing. On a pie chart of the budget, how many degrees larger is the salaries slice than the marketing slice?
questions.explanation: Salaries = 0.35 x 360 = 126 degrees and marketing = 0.2 x 360 = 72 degrees, so the difference is 54 degrees (or directly, 1,500,000/10,000,000 x 360). Option D is the difference in percentage points, option C is just the salaries angle, and option B divides by the marketing figure instead of the total.

questions.question: In a histogram with unequal class widths, bar heights are drawn as frequency density = frequency / class width so that areas are proportional to frequencies. A class '20 to under 40' kg has a frequency of 30. What is its frequency density?
questions.explanation: Class width = 40 - 20 = 20 kg, so frequency density = 30 / 20 = 1.5 per kg. Option C uses the raw frequency, which would exaggerate the wide class, option D uses a width of 19, and option B multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.question: A researcher wants a systematic sample of 60 customers from a list of 1,200. Using sampling interval k = N / n, what is k?
questions.explanation: k = N / n = 1,200 / 60 = 20, so every 20th customer is selected after a random start. Option B is the sample size itself, option D is the sampling fraction n / N, and option A subtracts instead of dividing.

questions.question: In a systematic sample with a sampling interval of 20, the randomly chosen starting point is item number 7. What is the item number of the 4th unit selected?
questions.explanation: The selected items are 7, 27, 47, 67, ..., so the 4th is 7 + (4 - 1) x 20 = 67. Option C adds one interval too many, option A multiplies the starting point by 4, and option B ignores the starting point.

questions.question: A firm has 300 junior staff, 150 senior staff and 50 managers. A stratified sample of 60 is drawn with PROPORTIONAL allocation (each group's share of the sample equals its share of the workforce). How many junior staff should be in the sample?
questions.explanation: Junior staff are 300 / 500 = 0.6 of the workforce, so the sample includes 0.6 x 60 = 36 junior staff.
